lessons.label: Carboxylic acid structure and acidity
lessons.title: Carboxylic acid structure and acidity
lessons.tag: Two oxygens stabilize the conjugate base

cards.rule: A carboxyl group has C=O and OH bonded to the same carbon. Carboxylic acids hydrogen bond and can dimerize, especially in nonpolar media. Their carboxylates are resonance stabilized. Electron-withdrawing substituents generally increase acidity, with inductive effects weakening over distance.
cards.cue: pH above pKa → more carboxylate. pH below pKa → more neutral acid.
cards.trap: The OH of COOH is not an ordinary alcohol group. When a carbon ring bears a COOH substituent, the carboxyl carbon is outside the ring, attached to a ring carbon. A lactone can have an endocyclic acyl carbon, but its group is a cyclic ester, not free COOH. Larger hydrocarbon regions can still limit aqueous solubility.
cards.app: Ionization controls how fatty acids, drug acids, and amino-acid side chains partition between environments.

steps.label: 1. Recognize COOH
steps.text: The acid functional group includes both oxygens and their shared carbon. Its carbon has no room for another carbon substituent beyond the existing skeleton.

steps.label: 2. Change pH
steps.text: Adjust pH around a model pKa of 4.8. At pH=pKa, [A−]=[HA]; two units above pKa gives a 100:1 ratio, about 99% A−.

diagram.caption: Acid/carboxylate speciation model; approximate dilute-solution treatment.

rule.title: Carboxylic Acid Centrosymmetric Dimers, Resonance Acidity & Inductive Distance Decay
rule.formula: RCOOH + NaHCO₃  →  RCOO⁻ Na⁺ + H₂O + CO₂(g)↑     (Diagnostic Fizzing Test for pKa < 6)

items.label: Dimeric Hydrogen Bonding
items.text: Pairs of carboxylic acids form cyclic 8-membered rings with TWO O–H···O=C hydrogen bonds, giving higher boiling points than alcohols of the same MW.

items.label: Inductive Substituent Effects
items.text: Electron-withdrawing groups stabilize RCOO⁻ and lower pKa: CF₃COOH (pKa 0.2) < CCl₃COOH (0.7) < ClCH₂COOH (2.9) < CH₃COOH (4.76). Effect decays rapidly with distance (α > β > γ)!

comparison: Delocalized over 1 O + 3 ring C atoms
Soluble in NaOH, insoluble in NaHCO₃
Delocalized equally over TWO O atoms
Soluble in weak NaHCO₃ (evolves CO₂↑ gas!)

figure.caption: Neutral acid versus carboxylate. The complete graphs retain all formal charges.

cue.title: Ranking Carboxylic Acid Acidity (pKa) on the MCAT
cue.prompt: What differs between the carboxylic acids you are ranking?

items.label: Halogen Electronegativity & Count
items.outcome: More Halogens & Higher EN → Lower pKa (Stronger Acid)
items.text: FCH₂COOH (pKa 2.6) is stronger than ClCH₂COOH (2.9) > BrCH₂COOH (2.9); Cl₃CCOOH (0.7) is much stronger than ClCH₂COOH (2.9).

items.label: Distance from –COOH (α vs. β vs. γ)
items.outcome: Closer to –COOH → Stronger Inductive Pull (α > β > γ)
items.text: 2-chlorobutanoic acid (pKa 2.8) > 3-chlorobutanoic acid (4.0) > 4-chlorobutanoic acid (4.5) > butanoic acid (4.8).

items.label: Dicarboxylic Acids (HOOC–(CH₂)_n–COOH)
items.outcome: pKa1 Is Lower Than 4.8; pKa2 Is Higher Than 4.8!
items.text: The neutral second –COOH acts as an inductive EWG to lower pKa1; once the first –COO⁻ forms, its −1 charge repels loss of the second H⁺ (raising pKa2).

trap.title: Drawing Carboxylate Resonance by Breaking the C–C Single Bond or Using Periodic Column Size for Inductive Effect

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Saying I–CH₂COOH is stronger than F–CH₂COOH because iodine is larger.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: In inductive effects (H is NOT attached to the halogen!), ONLY electronegativity matters: F > Cl > Br > I (size only dominates when the acidic H is bonded directly to X, as in HI vs HF)!

app.title: Amino Acid α-COOH pKa (~2.2) & Bicarbonate Extraction Separations

items.label: Why Amino Acid α-COOH Has pKa ~2.2 (Not 4.8)
items.outcome: Adjacent Protonated –NH₃⁺ Is a Powerful Inductive EWG!
items.text: The positively charged α-ammonium group pulls electron density away from the carboxylate, stabilizing –COO⁻ by >2.5 pKa units.

items.label: IR Broad "Hairy Beard" (2500–3300 cm⁻¹) + C=O (1710 cm⁻¹)
items.outcome: Unmistakable Carboxylic Acid IR Signature
items.text: Dimer O–H stretching creates a massive, ultra-broad trough from 2500 to 3300 cm⁻¹ overlapping the sp³ C–H peaks.

items.label: Citric Acid Cycle Intermediates
items.outcome: Citrate, Succinate, Malate Exist as Poly-Carboxylates at pH 7.4
items.text: All carboxylic acid groups (pKa 3–5) are >99% ionized at physiological pH 7.4.

lessons.label: Formation and acyl substitution
lessons.title: Formation and acyl substitution
lessons.tag: Activate the acid or use appropriate catalysis

cards.rule: Primary alcohols and aldehydes can be oxidized to acids. Fischer esterification combines acid and alcohol under acid catalysis; removing water or using excess alcohol drives the reversible reaction. Direct acid plus amine usually first gives an ammonium carboxylate salt; efficient amide synthesis generally requires activation or dehydrating conditions.
cards.cue: Proton transfer is often faster than acyl substitution. Check it before drawing a new amide bond.
cards.trap: OH− is a poor leaving group. Acid catalysis can enable water loss; coupling reagents or reactive acid derivatives can enable amide formation. Do not draw spontaneous amide synthesis just by mixing acid and amine in water.
cards.app: Peptide synthesis uses activated carboxyl groups; enzyme-catalyzed biosynthesis likewise supplies activation and organization.

steps.label: 1. Acid substrate
steps.text: The electrophilic acyl carbon is the carbonyl carbon. Protonating carbonyl oxygen increases electrophilicity in acid-catalyzed esterification.

steps.label: 2. Ester product pattern
steps.text: An ester has an OR group where the acid had OH. This example is ethyl propanoate: the O-ethyl and three-carbon acyl portions have different origins.

steps.label: 3. Amide product pattern
steps.text: An amide has N attached directly to the acyl carbon. Formation requires conditions that overcome acid–base salt formation and poor leaving-group ability.

rule.title: Carboxylic Acid Activation (SOCl₂, DCC/EDC), Fischer Esterification & Acyl Substitution

items.label: Addition–Elimination (Nucleophilic Acyl Substitution)
items.text: Unlike aldehydes/ketones (which lack a leaving group), carboxylic acids and derivatives undergo nucleophilic addition to a tetrahedral intermediate followed by ELIMINATION of the leaving group to restore C=O.

items.label: Converting –OH Into a Top-Tier Chloride (SOCl₂ or PCl₅)
items.text: Unactivated –OH is a poor leaving group; thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) converts RCOOH into highly reactive acid chloride RCOCl (driven by irreversible SO₂↑ + HCl↑ gas evolution).

items.label: Direct Amide Coupling Trap (Acid + Amine)
items.text: Mixing RCOOH + R′NH₂ immediately transfers a proton to give an unreactive salt (RCOO⁻ R′NH₃⁺); forming an amide at room temp requires activating –COOH first with SOCl₂ or carbodiimides (DCC/EDC)!

chips: RCOOH + R′NH₂ + Δ → Amide (Need EDC/DCC at RT!)
comparison: Forms unreactive carboxylate ammonium salt (RCOO⁻ R′NH₃⁺)
Forms amide bond at room temperature without heat
RCOOH + R′OH + Cat. H₂SO₄ ⇌ Ester + H₂O
Acyl C–O cleaves; alcohol O* ends up in ester!

figure.caption: Separate acid and ester examples; different carbon skeletons, not an esterification pair.

cue.title: Isotope Tracking (¹⁸O) & Equilibrium Control in Fischer Esterification
cue.prompt: What question is asked about Fischer esterification (RCOOH + R′¹⁸OH ⇌ RCO¹⁸OR′ + H₂O)?

items.label: Where Does the ¹⁸O Label on the Alcohol Go?
items.outcome: 100% into the Ester (R–CO–¹⁸OR′); Water Gets Unlabeled H₂O!
items.text: The alcohol oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon; the carboxylic acid –OH is protonated twice to leave as unlabeled H₂O.

items.label: How Do You Drive Reversible Fischer Esterification (K_eq ~ 1–4) to 100%?
items.outcome: Add Excess Alcohol OR Remove H₂O (Dean-Stark / Molecular Sieves)
items.text: By Le Chatelier’s principle, removing water or using the alcohol as solvent shifts equilibrium toward the ester.

items.label: Why Does tert-Butanol Fail in Standard Acid Fischer Esterification?
items.outcome: t-BuOH Forms a 3° Carbocation in Acid → Eliminates to Isobutylene!
items.text: Make tert-butyl esters by reacting t-BuOH with an acid chloride + pyridine (or reacting RCOOH with isobutylene).

trap.title: Assuming RCOOH + RNH₂ Forms an Amide Directly at Room Temperature

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Drawing a peptide/amide bond directly from RCOOH + R′NH₂ in water at 25 °C without a coupling reagent.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Amines (pKaH ~10) simply deprotonate carboxylic acids (pKa ~5) to form a stable carboxylate-ammonium salt; use EDC/DCC, SOCl₂, or biological ATP/aminoacyl-tRNA activation!

app.title: Aminoacyl-tRNA Synthetase ATP Activation & Acyl-CoA Thioesters

items.label: Biological Carboxylic Acid Activation
items.outcome: RCOO⁻ + ATP → Acyl-AMP (Mixed Anhydride) + PP_i
items.text: Cells never heat carboxylic acids withSOCl₂; instead, ATP adenylates the carboxylate into a reactive acyl-AMP intermediate before forming acyl-CoA or aminoacyl-tRNA.

items.label: EDC / NHS Crosslinking in Bioconjugation
items.outcome: Water-Soluble Carbodiimide for Protein Labeling
items.text: Links Asp/Glu carboxylates to Lys primary amines by converting –COO⁻ into an activated O-acylisourea ester.

items.label: Cyclic Esters (Lactones) & Amides (Lactams)
items.outcome: Intramolecular Fischer Esterification of γ/δ-Hydroxy Acids
items.text: 4-hydroxybutanoic acid or 5-hydroxypentanoic acid spontaneously cyclizes in acid to form stable 5-membered (γ) or 6-membered (δ) lactones.

lessons.label: Reduction and beta-keto-acid decarboxylation
lessons.title: Reduction and beta-keto-acid decarboxylation
lessons.tag: Track carbon atoms, not just functional groups

cards.rule: LiAlH4 followed by appropriate aqueous workup reduces a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol. Ordinary NaBH4 conditions generally do not. Heating a beta-keto acid can release CO2 through a favorable cyclic transition state, initially giving an enol that tautomerizes to a carbonyl.
cards.cue: Reduction retains the acid carbon. Decarboxylation loses it as CO2.
cards.trap: A beta-keto acid has a ketone at the beta position relative to the acid carbon. Not every carboxylic acid readily decarboxylates on heating. The six-membered arrangement is a transition state, not a stable ring intermediate.
cards.app: Decarboxylation changes carbon count, a useful check when following metabolic or synthetic pathways.

steps.label: 1. Number the beta-keto acid
steps.text: C1 is the carboxyl carbon, C2 is alpha, and C3 is the ketone-bearing beta carbon.

steps.label: 2. Lose the acid carbon
steps.text: The carboxyl carbon leaves as CO2. The remaining three-carbon fragment initially forms an enol, then becomes acetone by tautomerization.

rule.title: Carboxylic Acid Reduction (LiAlH₄ / BH₃) & Thermal β-Keto Acid Decarboxylation

items.label: Complete Reduction to 1° Alcohol (LiAlH₄ or BH₃·THF)
items.text: LiAlH₄ reduces RCOOH all the way to RCH₂OH; BH₃ (borane) selectively reduces carboxylic acids even in the presence of ketones or nitro groups!

items.label: Requirement for Thermal Decarboxylation (C=O at the β-Position!)
items.text: A carboxylic acid loses CO₂ upon gentle heating ONLY when a carbonyl (ketone, aldehyde, or second –COOH) sits at the β-carbon (3-oxocarboxylic acid / 1,3-dicarbonyl).

items.label: 6-Membered Cyclic Transition State → Enol → Ketone
items.text: Intramolecular H-bond between the –COOH proton and the β-C=O oxygen enables a concerted 6-electron pericyclic ring shift, releasing CO₂ gas and an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone.

comparison: Does NOT decarboxylate (would form unstable R⁻ carbanion)
Reduces all the way to 1° Alcohol (RCH₂OH)
Aldehyde intermediate is more reactive than acid (cannot stop!)

figure.caption: Heating a suitable beta-keto acid can release CO2, followed by tautomerization; schematic net pathway.

cue.title: Will This Carboxylic Acid Decarboxylate Upon Heating?
cue.prompt: Count from the carboxylic acid carbon (C1) to the other carbonyl:

items.label: Carbonyl at C3 (β-Keto Acid or Malonic Acid, 1,3-Relationship)
items.outcome: YES! Loses CO₂↑ Easily Upon Heating
items.text: Replace the entire –COOH group with –H! (Example: acetoacetic acid → acetone + CO₂↑; malonic acid → acetic acid + CO₂↑).

items.label: Carbonyl at C2 (α-Keto Acid) or C4 (γ-Keto Acid)
items.outcome: NO Thermal Decarboxylation Without an Enzyme
items.text: Cannot form the 6-membered cyclic transition state or stabilize the resulting α-enol/enolate; α-keto acids require TPP cofactor in biology.

items.label: Bridgehead Bicyclic β-Keto Acid (Bredt’s Rule Trap!)
items.outcome: NO Decarboxylation! (Bridgehead Cannot Form Planar Enol C=C)
items.text: Decarboxylation requires forming a Cα=Cβ enol double bond; if Cα is a rigid bicyclic bridgehead, Bredt’s rule forbids a bridgehead alkene!

trap.title: Decarboxylating Any Random Carboxylic Acid or Stopping LiAlH₄ at the Aldehyde

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Removing CO₂ from hexanoic acid or 4-oxopentanoic acid just because "Δ" is written over the arrow.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Only β-keto acids (3-oxo acids) and malonic acids (1,3-diacids) undergo spontaneous thermal decarboxylation via the 6-membered cyclic enol pathway!

app.title: Ketone Body Breath Acetone, Acetoacetic/Malonic Ester Synthesis & Citric Acid Cycle

items.label: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (Acetone Breath)
items.outcome: Acetoacetate (3-Oxobutanoate) → Acetone + CO₂↑
items.text: Acetoacetic acid is a β-keto acid that spontaneously decarboxylates in the blood and lungs, producing the fruity odor of acetone on the breath.

items.label: Isocitrate Dehydrogenase (TCA Cycle)
items.outcome: Oxalosuccinate (β-Keto Acid) → α-Ketoglutarate + CO₂↑
items.text: NAD⁺ first oxidizes the β-alcohol of isocitrate into a β-keto acid, setting up facile β-decarboxylation!

items.label: Malonic & Acetoacetic Ester Syntheses
items.outcome: 1. Base (NaOEt) → 2. R–X (SN2) → 3. H₃O⁺, Δ (−CO₂)
items.text: Temporarily uses an ester to acidify the α-CH₂ (pKa ~11) for clean alkylation, then hydrolyzes and decarboxylates off the extra carboxyl group.

cards.rule: Saponification is base-promoted ester hydrolysis, including hydrolysis of triacylglycerols to glycerol and fatty-acid salts. A fatty-acid carboxylate has a polar ionic head and a nonpolar hydrocarbon tail, allowing micelle formation under suitable conditions.
cards.cue: Head interacts with water; tails gather away from water.
cards.trap: Neutralizing a free fatty acid makes its salt, but that acid–base reaction is not ester hydrolysis. A micelle has hydrophobic material inside; it is not the same structure as a lipid bilayer.
cards.app: Soap can disperse nonpolar material into water through aggregates. Aggregation depends on concentration, ionic conditions, and tail structure.

steps.label: 1. Find the head group
steps.text: Laurate is a long-chain carboxylate. Its negative charge is represented on one O but delocalized over both. Counterions are omitted from this molecular-ion graph.

steps.label: 2. Contrast the tail
steps.text: The hydrocarbon tail interacts favorably with other nonpolar material. Many such tails can cluster while ionic heads contact the surrounding water.

rule.title: Saponification of Triacylglycerols, Irreversible Acid–Base Driving Force & Micelles

items.label: Step 1–2: Nucleophilic Addition of HO⁻ & Alkoxide Expulsion
items.text: Hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl to form a tetrahedral intermediate, which collapses by expelling the alkoxide (RO⁻) to form a carboxylic acid (RCOOH) andRO⁻.

items.label: Step 3: The Irreversible Acid–Base Driving Force!
items.text: Alkoxide (RO⁻, conjugate acid pKa ~16) immediately deprotonates the carboxylic acid (RCOOH, pKa ~5) to form a resonance-stabilized carboxylate (RCOO⁻, ΔpKa > 11 → K_eq > 10¹¹)!

items.label: Amphiphilic Self-Assembly (Micelles vs. Bilayers)
items.text: Single-tailed fatty acid salts (cone-shaped) pack into spherical MICELLES above the critical micelle concentration (CMC); double-tailed phospholipids (cylindrical) form planar BILAYERS.

chips: Micelle: Hydrophobic Tails In, –COO⁻ Heads Out
comparison: Step 1: HO⁻ attacks C=O → Step 2: RO⁻ leaves → Step 3: RO⁻ deprotonates RCOOH
Nonpolar tails dissolve grease inside core; ionic –COO⁻ heads face H₂O
Sulfonate detergents (R–SO₃⁻Na⁺) stay soluble in hard water

figure.caption: Aggregate cartoon: each head/tail token represents an amphiphile, not atoms or a resolved molecular structure.

cue.title: Why Saponification Is Irreversible & How Micelles Solubilize Oils
cue.prompt: What aspect of ester hydrolysis or lipid assembly is tested?

items.label: Why Is Base-Promoted Ester Hydrolysis Irreversible?
items.outcome: Final Deprotonation (RCOOH + RO⁻ → RCOO⁻ + ROH) Locks the Product!
items.text: Once the negatively charged carboxylate (RCOO⁻) forms, nucleophilic attack by ROH is electrostatically impossible; NaOH is a stoichiometric reagent, not a catalyst!

items.label: Single-Chain Soap vs. Double-Chain Phospholipid
items.outcome: 1 Chain (Cone) = Spherical Micelle; 2 Chains (Cylinder) = Bilayer
items.text: Steric packing geometry dictates whether an amphiphile forms a single-layer micelle core or a two-leaflet cell membrane.

items.label: What Drives Micelle Formation Thermodynamically?
items.outcome: Hydrophobic Effect: ↑ Entropy (ΔS > 0) of Released Bulk Water Molecules!
items.text: Burying nonpolar hydrocarbon tails releases ordered "clathrate cage" water molecules back into bulk water, increasing solvent entropy.

trap.title: Saying Hydrophobic Tails "Attract Each Other Strongly" as the Primary Driver of Micelles

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Claiming micelles form primarily because nonpolar tails have stronger attractions than water-water H-bonds.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: The hydrophobic effect is ENTROPY-driven (ΔS_water > 0): water molecules maximize their hydrogen-bonding freedom by excluding nonpolar chains into a shared core!

app.title: Bile Salt Emulsification, Pancreatic Lipase & Fatty Acid Melting Points

items.label: Bile Salts (Cholate / Chenodeoxycholate)
items.outcome: Facial Amphiphiles Emulsify Dietary Triacylglycerols
items.text: Break large fat globules into tiny mixed micelles in the duodenum, vastly increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase.

items.label: Saturated vs. Cis-Unsaturated Fatty Acids
items.outcome: More Carbons → ↑ MP; More Cis (Z) Double Bonds → ↓↓ MP
items.text: Stearic acid (18:0) is a waxy solid at 37 °C; oleic acid (18:1 cis-Δ⁹) and arachidonic acid (20:4) are liquids because cis kinks disrupt van der Waals packing.

items.label: Acid Workup After Saponification
items.outcome: RCOO⁻Na⁺ (Water-Soluble) + HCl → RCOOH (Organic-Soluble)
items.text: Adding strong acid protonates the soap carboxylate back into a neutral, water-insoluble free fatty acid.
